Critical FortiMail Zero-Day Flaw Exploited in Attacks Allows Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Writes
thehackernews.com · 02 Oct 2026 05:49 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGScisacve-2026-104286fortimailfortimail-7-2fortimail-7-4fortimail-7-6fortimail-8-0fortinetnull-byte-injectionpath-traversalunited-states
97
In plain words

U.S. cybersecurity officials warned that criminals are actively using a serious flaw in Fortinet FortiMail email-security systems. The flaw can let someone who does not have an account place files on an affected system, potentially changing how it works. Organizations using several FortiMail versions are affected and should install updates when available or limit access to the system’s management controls. The warning matters because attackers are already exploiting the issue, creating a risk of system takeover or disruption.

Summary
CISA added CVE-2026-104286, a critical FortiMail path-traversal and null-byte flaw that enables unauthenticated arbitrary file writes, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after active attacks were reported. Organizations should apply Fortinet’s updates when available or immediately disable IBE and restrict internet access to the FortiMail management interface.

CISA added CVE-2026-104286, a critical Fortinet FortiMail flaw, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reports of active exploitation. The vulnerability has a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects multiple FortiMail release branches. Fortinet acknowledged that the issue has been exploited in the wild. U.S. federal civilian agencies were recommended to apply patches or workarounds by October 4, 2026.

The flaw involves path traversal and improper handling of NULL characters, allowing unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Affected versions include FortiMail 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.6, 7.4.0–7.4.8, and 7.2.0–7.2.9. Until fixes are available for certain versions, Fortinet recommends disabling IBE support and restricting management-interface access to trusted private networks. Fortinet also provided indicators of compromise, including two IP addresses and a list of files that were added or modified.

  • The issue combines a directory-bypass weakness with mishandling of null characters, allowing file-writing through specially crafted web requests without requiring a login.
  • For some affected FortiMail versions, Fortinet’s fixed releases were still listed as upcoming, making the temporary mitigations—disabling IBE and limiting management access—immediately relevant.
  • Fortinet provided both suspected source IP addresses and a concrete list of added or modified files, enabling organizations to check systems for signs of compromise.
  • U.S. federal civilian agencies were directed to apply a patch or workaround by October 4, 2026, reflecting that the flaw is already being exploited in the wild.
Key Points
  • 01CISA added CVE-2026-104286, a critical Fortinet FortiMail vulnerability, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following reports of active exploitation.
  • 02The flaw has a CVSS score of 9.8 and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files to the underlying system through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests.
  • 03Affected releases include FortiMail 8.0.0 through 8.0.1, 7.6.0 through 7.6.6, 7.4.0 through 7.4.8, and 7.2.0 through 7.2.9.
  • 04Until fixes are available for certain versions, Fortinet recommends disabling IBE support and restricting FortiMail management-interface access to trusted private networks.
  • 05Fortinet shared indicators of compromise including IP addresses 79.141.169[.]187 and 45.129.0[.]192 and several added or modified files.

GitLab patched CVE-2026-90970, a critical AI Gateway vulnerability rated 9.9 out of 10, disclosed on October 2. Under certain conditions, a logged-in user with Duo Agent Platform access could use a specially crafted custom-flow configuration to escape a prompt-template sandbox and run arbitrary commands on a self-hosted gateway. The affected gateway is the service connecting a GitLab instance to AI models.

Only organizations that host their own AI Gateway need to act; GitLab said it has already patched gateways it hosts for GitLab.com, GitLab Dedicated, and applicable self-managed customers. Fixes are available in AI Gateway versions 19.2.4, 19.3.2, and 19.4.1, while no fixed release is listed for versions from 18.1.6 through the 19.1 line. GitLab listed no workaround or method to determine whether a gateway was previously attacked, and the article notes that a self-hosted gateway contains sensitive JWT signing keys and connects to both the GitLab instance and AI model providers.

  • Organizations running AI Gateway releases from 18.1.6 through the 19.1 line have no listed fixed version, and GitLab did not clarify whether the newer fixed gateway versions are compatible with older GitLab releases.
  • GitLab provided no workaround for organizations that cannot update and no method to determine whether a gateway was compromised before patching.
  • A successful command execution on a self-hosted gateway could be especially consequential because the gateway stores sensitive JSON Web Token signing keys and connects to both the GitLab instance and AI model providers.
  • This is GitLab's second critical AI Gateway template-engine issue in 2026: the February CVE-2026-1868 and CVE-2026-90970 are both classified as CWE-1336 weaknesses.

In plain words

A China-linked criminal group called Warlock broke into organizations by taking advantage of weaknesses in Microsoft SharePoint, a workplace file-sharing and collaboration system. Its recent targets included a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body, and a university in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking parts of Europe, Africa, and Latin America. The group disabled security software on many computers and then locked files with ransomware, which can disrupt essential services and force affected organizations to recover their systems.

Summary
China-linked Warlock ransomware operators are exploiting Microsoft SharePoint ToolShell vulnerabilities to breach critical organizations, then disabling AV/EDR protections and rapidly encrypting systems. Recent targets include water, telecom, government, and university entities in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking regions.

China-linked Warlock ransomware operators targeted a water utility, telecom provider, regional government body, and university by exploiting vulnerabilities in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint deployments. Symantec identifies the actor as Longlegs and attributes development of the Warlock ransomware to the group. Over the past two months, the activity appears to have focused on Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa, and Latin America.

In one intrusion that began on July 22, the attackers disabled protection software on at least 40 hosts in roughly two hours and deployed Warlock ransomware to at least 33 hosts. They used a signed K7RKScan driver vulnerable to CVE-2025-1055 to disable AV/EDR protections, staged the ransomware in the domain SYSVOL share, and installed Visual Studio Code Insiders as a service for remote connections through its tunneling feature. The ransomware appeared almost immediately after protections were disabled, and researchers warn that ToolShell and other SharePoint flaws remain viable ways for attackers to gain initial access.

  • The attackers used the SYSVOL share, which is replicated across domain controllers, to position ransomware for broad network-wide execution rather than deploying it to systems individually.
  • Warlock ransomware appeared almost immediately after security protections were disabled on each host, highlighting that the window between defense evasion and file encryption was very short in the observed incident.
  • The group installed Visual Studio Code Insiders as a service to use its built-in tunneling feature for remote access to compromised machines.
  • In the July 22 intrusion, the attackers conducted reconnaissance and deleted apparent staging artifacts two days after initial access, before the final ransomware deployment on July 31.
  • Although Warlock emerged exploiting SharePoint flaws more than a year earlier, Symantec and Carbon Black warn that ToolShell and other SharePoint vulnerabilities remain usable routes for initial access.
Key Points
  • 01The China-linked Warlock ransomware group targeted a water utility, telecom provider, regional government body, and university by exploiting vulnerabilities in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint deployments.
  • 02Symantec identifies the actor as Longlegs and attributes development of the Warlock ransomware to the group.
  • 03In an intrusion beginning July 22, the attackers deployed a tool that disabled protection software on at least 40 hosts in about two hours and then launched Warlock ransomware on at least 33 hosts.
  • 04The attackers used a signed K7RKScan driver vulnerable to CVE-2025-1055 to disable AV/EDR tools through the bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver technique.
  • 05The ransomware payload was staged in the domain SYSVOL share, and Visual Studio Code Insiders was installed as a service to enable remote connections through its built-in tunneling capability.

Pretty Themes, Hidden Loaders: GlassWorm-Linked Extensions Span VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX
socket.dev · 02 Oct 2026 03:44 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSaes-256-cbcaurora-nocturne-night-themecosmic-nebula-themesgithubglasswormmicrosoftopen-vsxrussiarussian-language-gatingsocketsolana-dead-drop-resolvervisual-studio-code-marketplace
88
In plain words

Researchers found that several downloadable color themes for VS Code and related editor marketplaces were connected to a group that had already used fake-looking themes to run harmful code. Two themes were confirmed to secretly download or run additional programs, while other related themes appeared harmless for now but still included code that a normal color theme would not need. Developers and organizations that installed these extensions could have exposed passwords, work accounts, cryptocurrency wallets, or files, showing that even simple-looking add-ons can be used to reach a person’s computer.

Summary
Socket linked a cluster of VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX theme extensions to the GlassWorm supply-chain campaign, including two confirmed malicious packages. The malicious extensions used hidden JavaScript loaders to download or dynamically execute attacker-controlled payloads, while related themes remained high-risk due to shared code, publisher, and development artifacts.

Socket Threat Research identified a cluster of VS Code theme extensions across the Visual Studio Marketplace and Open VSX that it assessed as associated with the GlassWorm campaign. The cluster included two confirmed malicious extensions, Aurora Nocturne Night Theme and Cosmic Nebula Themes, plus related themes such as Coca-Cola Christmas and Aurora Borealis Studio Theme. Although some related versions did not contain active payloads, Socket classified them as high-risk because they retained executable code unnecessary for ordinary color themes and shared development, publishing, and source-code links with confirmed malware.

Aurora Nocturne Night Theme hid an obfuscated Windows downloader that retrieved content from fingercakes4sale[.]store, wrote it to %TEMP%\\temp_batch.cmd, and ran it through cmd.exe. The Marketplace build of Cosmic Nebula Themes decrypted embedded JavaScript with AES-256-CBC, checked for Russian language and timezone conditions, used Solana transaction memos to obtain follow-on infrastructure, and executed remotely supplied JavaScript in memory. Socket linked this loader to GlassWorm with high confidence based on the shared Solana address, AES key, execution model, and cosmic-themes publisher namespace. Socket reported the live extensions to the marketplace operators, and the VS Code Marketplace removed the reported extensions shortly afterward.

  • A publicly visible source repository can appear benign while the extension package users actually install contains different, malicious runtime code, so reviewing only GitHub source is insufficient.
  • Cosmic Nebula Themes used Solana transaction memos to retrieve the address of its next payload stage, allowing the operator to change delivery infrastructure without publishing an updated extension.
  • The article shows that VS Code color themes can contain executable JavaScript and that VS Code does not provide granular controls to limit what that code can do, despite themes ordinarily needing only visual configuration.
  • Extensions without an active payload were still assessed as high-risk because they retained unnecessary executable functionality and shared publishing, code, and development links with confirmed malicious extensions.
Key Points
  • 01Socket identified a cluster of theme extensions spanning the Visual Studio Marketplace and Open VSX, with development and source-code links among Coca-Cola Christmas, Aurora Borealis Studio Theme, Aurora Nocturne Night Theme, and Cosmic Nebula Themes.
  • 02Aurora Nocturne Night Theme was a confirmed malicious Visual Studio Marketplace extension that downloaded content from fingercakes4sale[.]store, saved it as %TEMP%\temp_batch.cmd, and executed it through cmd.exe.
  • 03Socket confirmed that the Visual Studio Marketplace build of Cosmic Nebula Themes decrypted and executed embedded JavaScript, used Russian language and timezone checks, and queried a Solana address to resolve follow-on payload infrastructure.
  • 04Socket assessed Cosmic Nebula Themes as GlassWorm with high confidence because it shared a Solana address, AES key, staged execution model, and cosmic-themes publisher namespace with previously documented GlassWorm activity.
  • 05The Visual Studio Marketplace removed the reported live extensions after Socket's report, while Socket advised organizations that installed the confirmed malicious extensions to investigate for possible follow-on execution and exposed developer credentials.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete supply-chain malware investigation involving confirmed malicious VS Code Marketplace extensions and a high-confidence link to the GlassWorm developer-targeting campaign. It provides actionable indicators and shows that seemingly benign VS Code themes can execute staged payloads, affecting developers and organizations using VS Code or Open VSX extensions.

    In plain words

    Dell released updates for serious security problems in its Container Storage Modules software, which organizations use to connect data storage systems to Kubernetes computing clusters. The flaws could let an outsider access storage systems without a password, take administrator control, or gain full control of computers in an affected cluster. All versions before 1.17.0 are affected, and Dell says customers should update to version 1.18.0 and replace their token-signing secrets. If left unpatched, a single weakness could expose stored data and allow an attacker to bypass the access rules meant to protect an organization’s systems.

    Summary
    Dell patched critical flaws in Container Storage Modules that could let unauthenticated attackers gain storage administrator access or root control of Kubernetes cluster nodes. Organizations using CSM versions before 1.17.0 should upgrade to 1.18.0 and rotate JWT signing secrets.

    Dell released security updates for multiple critical flaws in Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM), affecting all versions before 1.17.0. The issues include missing authentication, hard-coded credentials and cryptographic keys, improper privilege management, and unsafe handling of template content. Dell says the flaws are fixed in CSM 1.18.0, with no workarounds or mitigations other than updating.

    Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-63688 and CVE-2026-63692, carry maximum CVSS scores of 10.0 and could allow unauthenticated attackers to obtain storage administrator credentials or administrative privileges. Other flaws could enable forged administrative tokens, root-level access on Kubernetes cluster nodes, access to Kubernetes Secrets, and unauthorized changes to cluster-wide access rules. Dell recommends that customers install the updates and rotate JWT signing secrets.

    • CVE-2026-63688 can bypass the CSM Authorization security model and expose administrator credentials for every registered storage array across five Dell storage product families.
    • A single custom resource submission exploiting CVE-2026-67269 could compromise every node in a Kubernetes cluster.
    • Publicly available hard-coded signing material associated with CVE-2026-61421 can enable unauthenticated attackers to forge administrator authentication tokens.
    • CVE-2026-67273 can provide cluster-wide access to Kubernetes Secrets and permit creation of cluster-wide access-control resources, bypassing intended Kubernetes restrictions.
    • Dell states that updating to CSM 1.18.0 is the only available remediation and also recommends rotating JWT signing secrets.
    Key Points
    • 01Dell released security updates for multiple critical vulnerabilities in Dell Container Storage Modules (CSM).
    • 02CVE-2026-63688 and CVE-2026-63692 have CVSS scores of 10.0 and could allow unauthenticated attackers to obtain storage administrator credentials or administrative-level privileges.
    • 03CVE-2026-67269 could allow a low-privilege remote attacker to gain root-level access on Kubernetes cluster nodes through a Custom Resource submission.
    • 04The affected flaws apply to all CSM versions before 1.17.0 and are addressed in version 1.18.0.
    • 05Dell recommends that customers update to the latest version and rotate any JWT signing secrets, as no other workarounds or mitigations are available.

In plain words

Dell fixed six severe security problems in software that helps its business storage systems work with Kubernetes, a platform companies use to run applications. The problems could let someone on the internet, without a username or password, take full control of storage systems, read sensitive stored access information, or access secret data used by applications. Organizations using Dell Container Storage Modules should update to version 1.18.0 or newer as soon as possible, because control of these systems could allow attackers to disrupt or manipulate data across many users.

Summary
Dell urges customers to immediately upgrade Container Storage Modules to version 1.18.0 or later to fix six critical flaws, including unauthenticated authentication-bypass bugs that could give remote attackers full control of storage infrastructure and Kubernetes cluster resources.

Dell has patched six critical vulnerabilities in its Container Storage Modules (CSM), software that connects Dell enterprise storage arrays to Kubernetes environments. Two maximum-severity flaws in the CSM Authorization module, CVE-2026-63688 and CVE-2026-63692, stem from missing authentication for critical functions. Dell recommends customers upgrade to CSM version 1.18.0 or later at the earliest opportunity.

CVE-2026-63688 could let an unauthenticated remote attacker access administrator credentials for all registered storage arrays and gain full control of the storage infrastructure. CVE-2026-63692 affects the authorization proxy and tenant service and could allow attackers to bypass authentication and obtain administrator privileges across tenants. The four other critical flaws could enable unauthenticated attackers to gain root access on cluster nodes, administer the authorization proxy, forge authentication tokens, or gain cluster-wide read access to Kubernetes Secrets.

Dell has not said that the newly disclosed CSM vulnerabilities are being actively exploited. In plain words

The article reports that people can install an app called Peer2Profit to earn small amounts of money by letting others use their internet connection, and that this connection can then be sold through AstroProxy. Researchers showed that a paying customer could use one such connection to reach a Portuguese home router’s settings page and download a file, even without the router owner’s login details. This can affect homes and businesses because traffic from fraud or other abuse may appear to come from their internet address, and people buying access may be able to reach devices inside the same network. The broader concern is that these programs may look legitimate to security software, making the problem difficult to notice before damage or disruption occurs.

Summary
Silent Push found that bandwidth-sharing apps such as Peer2Profit can turn home or corporate-connected devices into AstroProxy exit nodes, allowing subscribers to route traffic through them and potentially reach internal network resources via a DNS-based filter bypass. The risk is hard to detect because the software is often installed with user consent and is not typically flagged by endpoint security tools.

Silent Push published research describing how Peer2Profit, a bandwidth-sharing program, can supply residential connections to AstroProxy, which sells them as commercial proxy access. In controlled testing, researchers enrolled a clean residential IP address in Peer2Profit and saw it appear in AstroProxy’s enumeration data within roughly ten minutes. AstroProxy sells residential traffic at \(7.60 per gigabyte, while Peer2Profit’s stated residential rate is \)0.28 per gigabyte; Silent Push calculated the operation retains more than 97% of the sale value.

Over 72 hours, Silent Push observed 117,224 unique IP addresses across AstroProxy’s residential, datacenter, and mobile pools, with residential addresses increasing by an average of 1,071 per hour. The researchers also bypassed AstroProxy’s filter against direct internal-IP requests by using a domain name that resolved to an internal MEO router-management address, then accessed the interface and downloaded a file. The article says this could expose organizations to traffic that appears to originate from their own IP addresses and potentially make internal resources reachable through a device enrolled in a proxy pool, while ordinary antivirus and reputation tools may not identify the bandwidth-sharing software as malicious.

  • The economics heavily favor the proxy operator: Silent Push calculated that AstroProxy retains more than 97% of the value from bandwidth sold through the Peer2Profit arrangement.
  • Rapid address turnover weakens reputation-based blocking because residential nodes were added at an average rate of 1,071 per hour, often rotating before an address can build a useful abuse history.
  • AstroProxy customers can filter available nodes by country, city, network provider, and connection type, allowing them to select connections that are geographically or network-wise close to a target.
  • The article identifies a practical insurance and business-risk question that ordinary endpoint tools may not answer: whether any device on an applicant’s network is currently selling bandwidth through a proxy pool.
  • A company can face consequences even if it is not directly compromised, because fraudulent or abusive activity routed through its connection can cause its public internet address to be placed on blocklists.
Key Points
  • 01Silent Push reported that Peer2Profit pays users to share bandwidth and that enrolled residential IP addresses appeared in AstroProxy’s proxy pool within roughly ten minutes during controlled testing.
  • 02Over a 72-hour crawl, Silent Push observed 117,224 unique IP addresses across three AstroProxy pools, including 60,247 residential addresses, with the residential pool adding an average of 1,071 new addresses per hour.
  • 03Silent Push demonstrated that AstroProxy’s direct internal-IP filtering could be bypassed with a domain name that resolved to a MEO router’s internal management address, allowing researchers to access the interface and download a file.
  • 04The article states that bandwidth-sharing clients are often deliberately installed through official channels and may not be flagged by antivirus or standard threat-intelligence and reputation systems.
  • 05Silent Push said it had not confirmed an incident in which a bandwidth-sharing client was the entry point, although its researchers characterized the demonstrated internal-network access as a potential route to one.

This is a concrete, recent research finding showing that commercially sold residential proxy access could enable access to internal router interfaces through a DNS-based bypass. It has broad relevance because voluntarily installed bandwidth-sharing software may evade standard endpoint and reputation-based controls, although no confirmed incident using this as an entry point was reported.

Summary
Cloudflare launched protected Quick Tunnels in cloudflared 2026.9.3, allowing developers to restrict accountless trycloudflare.com tunnels to specified email addresses or domains using Cloudflare Access one-time PIN verification. Authorization rules remain locally in cloudflared, so Cloudflare verifies identity without receiving the tunnel’s guest list.

Cloudflare introduced protected Quick Tunnels in cloudflared 2026.9.3 through the --allowed-mail flag. Developers can restrict a temporary trycloudflare.com URL to specific email addresses or domains without creating a Cloudflare account, configuring DNS, or using a dashboard. Visitors authenticate by entering a one-time PIN sent to their email through Cloudflare Access. Public Quick Tunnels remain unchanged when the flag is not used.

Protected tunnels are intended for developers and coding-agent workflows that need to share services running locally without exposing them to anyone who obtains the link. Cloudflare Access verifies that a visitor controls an email address, while the local cloudflared process compares that verified address against the developer’s allowed-email rules. The guest list remains on the developer’s machine, and Cloudflare receives the authentication mode but not the authorization rules. After authentication, cloudflared creates a local session for up to four hours, strips authentication credentials before forwarding traffic to the local app, and ends access when the cloudflared process stops.

  • Protected Quick Tunnels separate identity checking from permission decisions: Cloudflare Access confirms email ownership, but the local cloudflared process compares that verified address against the developer’s private guest list.

  • The authentication handoff is delivered through a form submission rather than a URL, preventing it from appearing in browser history, URLs, or logs.

58
In plain words

Trail of Bits introduced SequenceHash and SequenceMAC, free tools and specifications that help developers safely combine several pieces of data into one digital fingerprint. They prevent different sets of inputs, such as separate words versus the same words joined together, from accidentally producing the same result. This matters to developers of cryptographic software, including systems that verify cryptocurrency transactions or make private digital proofs, because unclear data boundaries can enable forgery or let a commitment be interpreted in more than one way.

Summary
Trail of Bits released SequenceHash and SequenceMAC, open specifications and implementations for securely hashing multiple variable-length inputs with standard hash functions such as SHA-256 and BLAKE. The constructions use unambiguous length encoding, domain-separation customization strings, and double hashing to prevent input-boundary ambiguity and length-extension issues.

Trail of Bits introduced SequenceHash and SequenceMAC through the Community Cryptography Specification Project, with initial Rust, Go, and Python implementations plus test vectors. The constructions are intended to safely hash multiple values together when developers use hash functions other than Keccak, including SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, BLAKE, and RIPEMD. They address the problem that repeated calls to a normal hash update function are effectively just concatenation, so different input boundaries can produce the same hash input.

SequenceHash encodes every input with a fixed 128-bit byte-length suffix, ensuring that separate inputs cannot be confused with a different grouping or concatenation of the same bytes. It also uses a double-hash structure to prevent length-extension issues and supports optional customization strings for binding the same inputs to different contexts without rehashing the inner data. SequenceMAC adds a keyed mode requiring keys of at least 32 bytes and includes key-length metadata to avoid HMAC-style key pseudocollisions, such as treating keys with appended zero bytes as equivalent.

The article says ambiguous input encoding can create risks in Fiat-Shamir transforms, cryptographic commitments, file archives, cryptocurrency transaction grouping, and other uses where variable-length values must be hashed together. TupleHash already solves this problem for Keccak, but the article notes that it is not defined for other hash functions and that simply replacing Keccak can remove important security properties. SequenceHash and SequenceMAC are presented as focused tools rather than a complete solution: developers must still encode complex values consistently, include all required protocol inputs, and select hash outputs appropriate for their intended use.

  • Calling a normal hash function’s update method multiple times does not preserve the boundaries between values, because the hash ultimately processes the same concatenated byte stream.
  • TupleHash is a strong existing solution, but it is defined for Keccak; simply substituting another hash function can remove important protections such as resistance to length extension.
  • SequenceHash places customization strings only in its outer hash layer, so applications can derive context-specific results from the same inputs without recalculating the inner hash.
  • HMAC can treat a key and that same key followed by zero bytes as equivalent in some cases, while SequenceMAC includes key-length metadata so trailing zeros remain meaningful.
  • Even with unambiguous hashing, developers must ensure all parties serialize complex values consistently, since formats such as JSON and XML may not guarantee field ordering.
Key Points
  • 01Trail of Bits introduced SequenceHash and SequenceMAC, hash constructions specified through the Community Cryptography Specification Project and initially implemented in Rust, Go, and Python.
  • 02SequenceHash uses fixed 128-bit byte-length suffixes to encode each input separately, preventing distinct sequences of inputs from being treated as the same concatenated data.
  • 03The constructions use double hashing to prevent length-extension issues in underlying hash functions such as SHA-256 and SHA-512.
  • 04SequenceHash supports optional customization strings that bind identical inputs to different contexts while allowing the inner hash to be reused.
  • 05SequenceMAC is a keyed variant requiring keys of at least 32 bytes and includes key-length metadata to avoid HMAC-style key pseudocollisions, including trailing-zero key equivalence.

In plain words

The article compares tools that help organizations find and fix weak spots in their software, online services, and computer systems. This matters because criminals are increasingly using those weak spots to break in, and the article says known software flaws were involved in about 31% of breaches in Verizon’s 2026 report. Companies need tools that help their developers or IT teams focus on the problems most likely to be abused and quickly apply safe fixes, rather than leaving large piles of alerts unresolved.

Summary
Vulnerability remediation tools differ most in whether they merely identify and prioritize findings or actually help deploy fixes, such as pull requests, dependency upgrades, or patches. The article positions Aikido as a code-to-cloud option focused on exploitability-based triage and automated developer workflow remediation.

The article compares six vulnerability remediation tools for 2026: Aikido Security, Snyk, GitHub Advanced Security, Tenable, Qualys, and Wiz. It argues that the main challenge for engineering teams is increasingly fixing weaknesses rather than finding them, as frontier models surface vulnerabilities faster than teams can validate them. It cites Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, which found that vulnerability exploitation was involved in roughly 31% of breaches and that median time to full patching reached 43 days.

The comparison focuses on coverage, risk prioritization, remediation capability, deployment, and ownership of fixes. Aikido, Snyk, and GitHub offer developer-focused remediation such as pull requests for dependency upgrades or suggested code fixes, while Qualys includes built-in patch deployment for infrastructure and Tenable generally relies on integrations and patch tooling. Wiz prioritizes cloud issues through attack-path context but generally provides guidance and ticketing rather than performing the fix itself.

The article says effective prioritization should go beyond severity ratings by considering whether code is reachable, whether a public proof of concept exists, exploit prediction scores, and whether a service is exposed to the internet. It warns that automated dependency upgrades can break builds when they require major-version changes and that some flaws have no upstream patch. It also emphasizes that findings should appear in developers’ existing workflows and be verified by rescanning after remediation, rather than simply being closed as tickets.

  • The article identifies remediation, rather than finding vulnerabilities, as the engineering bottleneck as frontier models surface flaws faster than teams can validate them.
  • Severity scores alone can misdirect effort because a high-severity issue in unreachable code may be less urgent than a lower-severity issue exposed to the internet.
  • Automated dependency upgrades are not always safe: upgrades that cross a major version can break builds, and some vulnerabilities have no patched upstream release.
  • Tools that place findings outside developers’ normal code-review and development workflow risk being ignored by the people responsible for fixing them.
  • A unified code-to-cloud platform can reduce duplicate alerts when a single underlying problem appears across code, containers, infrastructure definitions, and cloud settings.

In plain words

The article says company security leaders often cannot clearly tell their boards how safe the business is, how much money could be at risk, or whether things have improved, because important information is scattered across many separate security systems. This can hide a chain of small access problems that together could let someone reach sensitive customer data or other critical company systems. It matters because boards need clear information to decide where to spend money and reduce the risks that could cause serious business harm.

Summary
The article argues that CISOs should replace activity-based board metrics with unified, attack-path-based reporting that connects identity, cloud, SaaS, endpoint, and data context to quantify exposure to critical assets. It promotes Mesh Security’s cybersecurity mesh approach as a way to show financial risk and quarter-over-quarter risk reduction.

The article argues that traditional board-level security reporting relies too heavily on activity counts, such as vulnerabilities found or alerts closed, instead of showing business exposure. Boards instead want to know which critical assets are reachable, whether that exposure is declining, and what the possible financial impact would be. Security leaders often struggle to answer because relevant information is distributed among separate identity, cloud, endpoint, SaaS, SIEM, and vulnerability-management tools.

The article describes how several moderate findings across different systems can form a critical path to sensitive data, even when no individual dashboard shows the full chain. It recommends identifying the organization’s most important assets with business owners, connecting existing data sources, mapping real paths to those assets, and prioritizing fixes by their potential impact. It presents Cybersecurity Mesh Architecture and Mesh’s agentless integrations as a way to correlate existing security-tool data and report the number of attack paths eliminated from one quarter to the next.

  • Several individually moderate findings can combine into a critical route to sensitive data, such as a leftover contractor permission, a SaaS-to-cloud integration, and a broadly privileged service account.
  • A medium-severity configuration issue on a route to customer data may deserve higher priority than a critical software flaw on an isolated test server because it has a larger potential impact.
  • Identifying critical assets with business owners, rather than security staff alone, gives security reporting a business-defined basis for deciding which exposures matter most.
  • Tracking the number of reachable paths to critical assets from quarter to quarter can show both whether risk is declining and which remediation efforts produced that reduction.
  • AI agents, service accounts, non-human identities, and MCP-connected tools can create additional access paths faster than organizations inventory them.
Key Points
  • 01Boards want security reporting that shows exposure to business-critical assets, changes in exposure over time, and the financial impact of potential compromise rather than counts of security activities.

  • 03The article describes Cybersecurity Mesh Architecture as a common intelligence layer that correlates data from existing security tools to connect identities, access, assets, and exposures.
  • 04The proposed reporting framework starts by identifying critical business assets, mapping real paths to those assets, and prioritizing fixes by the potential impact they prevent.

prompts concept
